en: Cotton became the boom crop, known as the plant of gold, and by about 1600 it had driven out sugar, whose Cypriot plantations were already failing against Madeira, a competitor the Venetian diarist Marino Sanudo named as early as 1496. Salt from Larnaca was a state monopoly so strict that Venetian ships calling at the island had to dump their ballast and load salt for Venice, and John Locke reported in 1553 that a Venetian caught carrying an ounce out of the city lost an ear; estimates of what the Signory made from it range from 100,000 to 800,000 ducats a year, and Hill thought 300,000 near the truth. Grain was the largest crop of all, its export licensed only after eighteen months' supply had been set aside, and the Proveditor Bernardo Sagredo reckoned the island's whole revenue in 1585 at 546,000 ducats, of which 300,000 came from salt, leaving 361,669 net of the garrison's pay; fortification swallowed much of the rest, 178,092 ducats going on Famagusta between 1491 and 1528 and the Martinengo bastion alone costing 50,000.

en: Italian, and specifically the Venetian dialect, became the written language of government, and by 1531 the Assizes had been rendered into it; a French visitor named Mesenge complained in 1507 that pleadings once made in French were now made in Italian, and that Cypriot gentlemen, as good Frenchmen as any in France, were wonderfully ill content to be subjects of Venice. Greek remained the language of the countryside and of the church. The chronicles of the transition make the point neatly, Georgios Boustronios writing his account of 1456 to 1489 in Cypriot Greek prose while his relative Florio Bustron, an administrator under Venice, wrote his Historia overo commentarii de Cipro in Italian, and the 156 Petrarchan poems in Cypriot Greek preserved in the Marciana were probably assembled between 1546 and 1570.

en: The Latin church stayed on top and the Greek church stayed subordinate, with four bishops each answering to the Latin diocesan above him and the Greek archbishopric still vacant under the terms of the Bulla Cypria. Nicholas Coureas argues that in practice the Greek church grew stronger rather than weaker, because the Latins were few and town bound, Rome was distant and the Ottoman threat made enforcement of papal directives unwise; the four Greek bishops drew 1,400 ducats between them about 1500, while eighteen Greek monasteries were reported in 1529 with 6,600. The Maronites lost people back to the Levant under heavy taxation, and the Armenians dwindled too, though they had held their Nicosia quarter and the church of Notre Dame de Tyre since before 1504 and kept shops in Famagusta, Limassol, Paphos and the capital.
ctx: era Venetian: life/religion

en: Venetian reports put the island's population somewhere between 100,000 and 200,000 and disagree wildly among themselves: 106,000 from the Cypriot deputation of 1490, 90,000 from the Syndic of 1504 against his Lieutenant's 130,000, 121,179 in the census of 1523, 126,179 from Minio in 1529, 197,000 from Attar about 1540 and 200,000 from Graziani about 1570, on which evidence Hill concluded the population probably rose rather than fell. Serfdom was the ordinary condition: Martin von Baumgarten wrote in 1508 that all the inhabitants were slaves to the Venetians, paying a third of everything and working two days a week for the state, and Hill computes the paroikoi's burden at about forty per cent of produce, a third plus the tithe; every villein, male or married female over fifteen, also paid a besant a head for salt, and in 1490 the Cypriots said many had fled the island rather than bear it. Nicosia held perhaps 21,000 people before the siege of 1570 and roughly that number died in it, the Ottoman survey of 1572 finding between 1,100 and 1,200 left; Famagusta held out from September 1570 to 5 August 1571, and contemporaries put the total Venetian and Cypriot loss at 56,000 killed or enslaved.

en: The Porte farmed the island out, first through timars granted to Lala Mustafa's soldiers and later through annual iltizam and lifetime malikane leases, and the cizye or poll tax on non-Muslims was set in 1572 at eleven, five and a half or three piastres according to means. The imperial rescript of 1754 fixed the island's liability at 10,066 warrants of assessment at twenty-one and a half piastres each, some 216,400 piastres a year, and required that number to be issued whether the population rose or fell; by the 1760s barely 7,500 people were left to pay it, which explains eighteenth century Cyprus better than anything else does. Cotton was the chief export, about 3,000 quintals or 750 tons a year around 1750 going to Britain, France, Holland and Venice, with the French houses at Larnaca acting as factors for merchants of Marseille; Mahmud II fixed the annual tribute at 3,179,082 piastres in 1837, and a British consular return of the 1870s puts total regular revenue at 16,836,874 piastres, of which the salt monopoly alone yielded 2,929,550.
ctx: era Ottoman: life/economy

en: Ottoman Turkish was the language of administration and of the kadi courts, which non-Muslims and foreigners could also use, while Greek remained the language of the great majority and of the church that collected their taxes. Cypriot Turkish grew out of Ottoman Turkish and the Yoruk dialect of the Taurus, brought by settlers moved from the Karaman region under the settlement law of 22 September 1572, and Sir Harry Luke thought the community had preserved the purity of its Turkish to a degree matched almost nowhere else; the British census of 1881 found 95 per cent of the island's Muslims giving Turkish as their mother tongue, the Greek-speaking remainder falling below two per cent by the 1920s. No literacy rate for Ottoman Cyprus appears to survive, but Archbishop Kyprianos founded the Hellenic School of Nicosia in 1812, the island's first secondary school and now the Pancyprian Gymnasium.

en: The Latin church was suppressed after 1571 and the Orthodox archbishopric restored, Timotheos taking office in 1572 as the first Greek archbishop since 1260, while Saint Sophia in Nicosia and Saint Nicholas in Famagusta became mosques, taking the names Selimiye and Lala Mustafa Pasha only in 1954. Under the millet system the archbishop and his three suffragans rose from spokesmen for their flock, a role the chronicler Kyprianos dates to about 1660, to being the tax intermediaries of the settlement of 1754, so that one British traveller reported that Cyprus was in fact governed by the Greek archbishop and his clergy; that ascendancy ended on 9 July 1821, when the governor Kucuk Mehmet had Archbishop Kyprianos and the three bishops killed along with some 470 to 486 leading Greeks, the count varying by source. Latins, Venetians, Maronites and Armenians converted to Islam to escape the taxes and disabilities laid on non-Muslims and became the Linobambaki, the linen and cotton people who kept a Christian and a Muslim name apiece across seventeen to twenty villages depending on which list one follows, while at Larnaca the Hala Sultan Tekke grew around the tomb of Umm Haram, a shrine built in 1760 with its mosque completed in 1817.
ctx: era Ottoman: life/religion

en: The conquest emptied the island: 76 villages of the Mesaoria and Mazato were recorded with no inhabitants at all in 1572, Nicosia fell from perhaps 21,000 people to between 1,100 and 1,200, and famine followed the war. The enumerations counted taxpayers rather than people and must be read as such, an examiner about 1641 finding hardly 25,000 rayahs after the dearth of 1640 and the plague of 1641, Archimandrite Kyprianos publishing the census of 1777 as 10,487 Christian tax-paying families in 564 villages, giving 37,000 Christians and 47,000 Muslims while warning that the estimate was approximate and that doubts about the Muslim figure were grave, and the Ottoman register of 1831, which counted males only, returning 14,983 Muslim and 29,190 non-Muslim males, 44,216 in all. Plague took perhaps a third of the island in 1692 and again in 1760, drought and locusts brought a famine in 1757 and 1758 that sent a great number fleeing to Syria and Anatolia, and the tax revolt of 1764 ended with the muhassil Cil Osman and eighteen of his followers killed in the burning palace; the first British census, taken in 1881 three years after the handover, found 186,173 people, 137,631 of them Greek Orthodox and 45,458 Muslim.

en: Under the Cyprus Convention Britain undertook to pay the Ottoman treasury an annual fixed sum of 92,799 pounds, eleven shillings and threepence, more than half the island's average revenue, but the money never reached Istanbul: it was deposited at the Bank of England to service the Ottoman Crimean War loan of 1855 on which the Porte had defaulted, and it was Cypriots who paid both the tribute and the cost of their own administration. Churchill, visiting as Undersecretary in 1907, wrote that Britain had no right except by force majeure to take a penny of the Cyprus Tribute to relieve itself of its own obligations, and Parliament soon voted a permanent grant-in-aid of 50,000 pounds which reduced it accordingly. Copper came back with the Cyprus Mines Corporation, founded in 1916 after Charles Gunther noticed the Roman slag at Skouriotissa, and by 1955 its mines were the island's largest industry and furnished more than a quarter of all government revenue; asbestos was worked at Amiantos in the Troodos until 1988, the Cyprus Government Railway carried 3,199,934 tons of freight between 1905 and 1951 without ever making a profit, and by the 1960s Britain was drinking 13.6 million litres of Cypriot wine a year, half the island's production and most of it sold as sweet sherry.

en: English was the official language of the colony and continued in legal proceedings until 1989 and in the legislature until 1963, though Greek and Turkish remained in everyday and communal use. Schooling was divided between Greek and Turkish curricula, and British attempts to curtail Greek influence in the schools were among the stated causes of the revolt of 1931. No literacy rate from the colonial censuses could be traced for this entry, but the growth of Greek secondary education is plain enough in the expansion of the Nicosia Hellenic School into a lyceum in 1893 and the founding of a teacher training college the following year.
ctx: era British Cyprus: life/language

en: The Church of Cyprus kept its standing and its politics, and the archbishop remained the ethnarch: Makarios III was elected on 18 September 1950 and the church at once organised the enosis plebiscite of that January, signed in open books placed in the churches, which returned 95.7 per cent in favour, a result taken by some as coerced. Muslim religious property was administered through the Evkaf, over which the 1878 Convention gave Britain a measure of control, with an Ottoman and a British delegate on a board that also seated the mufti and the kadi of Cyprus; Britain gave up that control only in 1956. The church then led the political struggle, Makarios becoming the political head of the EOKA campaign from 1955 and being exiled to the Seychelles in 1956.

en: The censuses run every ten years from 1881, with none taken in 1941, and show steady growth: 186,173 in 1881, 237,022 in 1901, 347,959 in 1931, 450,114 in 1946 and 573,566 in 1960, the Greek Orthodox share rising from 73.9 per cent to about 80 by 1946 before settling at 77.1 in 1960, and the Muslim or Turkish share falling from 24.4 per cent to 18.2. Emigration ran outward throughout, with some 30,000 Turkish Cypriots leaving for Turkey between 1881 and 1927 and a Turkish Cypriot community of about 8,500 established in Britain by 1958. The October 1931 riots left seven protesters dead and 2,606 people punished, nine camps at Caraolos, Dhekelia and Xylotymbou held 53,510 Jewish detainees between August 1946 and January 1949, and the malaria campaign begun in 1946 by the Turkish Cypriot health inspector Mehmet Aziz divided the island into 556 blocks and made Cyprus the first malaria-free country in the world by February 1950.

en: The events of 1974 cost the Republic about seventy per cent of its wealth-producing resources, tourist facilities falling by 65 per cent and industry by 46, after which growth averaged 6.1 per cent a year through the 1980s. Services now account for close to eighty per cent of the economy and agriculture for about two, and travel and tourism generate roughly a fifth of GDP, arrivals passing four million for the first time in 2024 and earning about 3.2 billion euros, with the United Kingdom, Israel and Poland the largest markets; the shipping registry is the third largest in the European Union. The euro replaced the Cypriot pound on 1 January 2008 at 0.585274 to one, and the banking crisis of March 2013 brought a ten billion euro programme, the closure of Laiki and the conversion of 47.5 per cent of uninsured deposits at the Bank of Cyprus into shares, some 3.8 billion euros in all; halloumi was registered as a protected designation of origin in 2021 under all three of its names, and the Aphrodite gas field, announced in December 2011, is not expected to produce before 2027.

en: Article 3 of the 1960 constitution makes Greek and Turkish the official languages, requires legislative and administrative acts to be drawn up in both, and allows anyone to address the authorities in either. In practice Standard Modern Greek is the high variety and Cypriot Greek, which is unintelligible to an unprepared speaker of the standard, is the language people actually use, and Cypriot Turkish stands in much the same relation to standard Turkish in the north, where the standard became the language of schools and media. English remains widely spoken, by about 73 per cent of the population according to Eurobarometer, and it served in the courts until 1989; Armenian was recognised under the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages on 1 December 2002 and Cypriot Maronite Arabic in 2008, though at the 2011 census none of the 3,656 Maronite Cypriots in the government-controlled area declared it as a first language.

en: Makarios III held the archbishopric and the presidency at once from 1960 until his death in 1977, and when three bishops demanded that he resign the presidency in 1972 he had them defrocked the following summer and enlarged the synod to dilute them. The constitution gives special standing to five bodies, the Church of Cyprus, the Vakif, the Maronites, the Armenian Orthodox and the Latins, and provides that citizens belonging to neither main community must opt to join one of them: the Armenians, recognised as a religious group under Article 2, chose the Greek Cypriot community in a referendum on 13 November 1960. The 2011 census gave the government-controlled area as 89.1 per cent Greek Orthodox among all residents, or 97.4 per cent among Cypriot citizens alone, and the 2021 figure of 74.5 per cent looks like a collapse but chiefly reflects a rise in those declining to state a religion, from 1.1 to 17.3 per cent; the Technical Committee on Cultural Heritage has meanwhile restored or protected more than a hundred churches and mosques on both sides of the line.
ctx: era Republic of Cyprus: life/religion

en: The 1960 census found 573,566 people, 77.1 per cent Greek and 18.2 per cent Turkish, and in the fighting of 1963 and 1964 nearly 25,000 Turkish Cypriots, about a sixth of their community, left their homes for enclaves, Pierre Oberling's figures giving 364 Turkish Cypriot and 174 Greek Cypriot dead. In 1974 between 140,000 and 200,000 Greek Cypriots were displaced from the north, the spread reflecting the difference between people counted crossing and the refugee caseload the government supported, and 50,000 to 60,000 Turkish Cypriots moved north from the south, largely under the Vienna III agreement of August 1975; the Committee on Missing Persons lists 2,002 people missing from 1963 to 1974, 1,510 Greek Cypriots and 492 Turkish Cypriots, of whom 1,081 had been identified by July 2026. The 2021 census counted 923,381 residents in the government-controlled area, 77.9 per cent of them Cypriot citizens, with Greeks, Romanians, Britons, Bulgarians, Syrians and Russians the largest foreign groups, so that about a fifth of the population holds another nationality; the north's last agreed census, in 2011, gave 286,257, and the number of settlers from Turkey remains genuinely contested, the researcher Mete Hatay calling the higher claims wildly speculative.
